analysis.one_liner: Ends the federal tax deduction employers claim for spending to fight union organizing.
analysis.headline: The bill won support from 29 Democratic-aligned senators but never received a hearing or vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the tax code so that money employers spend trying to influence their employees about unions — anti-union campaigns, captive-audience meetings, and consultants — would no longer be a deductible business expense, ending what the bill calls a taxpayer subsidy for those campaigns. It would also require employers to report such spending to the IRS, with penalties up to $1,000 per employee for failing to do so. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers deciding whether to form or join a union. Employer campaigns against organizing would cost more since they could no longer be written off as a business expense, and the spending would have to be disclosed to the IRS, making it public. Taxpayers also benefit, because they stop effectively subsidizing employer anti-union spending.

how_it_helps.text: Denies employers a tax deduction for expenditures aimed at influencing their employees about labor organizations, labor elections, labor disputes, and collective action, extending the existing rule that political spending is not deductible [S2][S3].
Requires employers to report their spending on such efforts to the IRS, with a penalty of the greater of $10,000 or $1,000 per full-time employee, rising up to $100,000 for continued failures [S3].

Cites Economic Policy Institute findings that employers were charged with unfair labor practices in roughly 4 of 10 union elections in 2016-2017 and that companies spent $340 million a year on outside consultants to sway workers' opinions about union activity [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that run anti-union campaigns — they would pay the full cost of consultants, captive-audience meetings, and legal fees without a tax break, and would face new reporting requirements and potential IRS penalties. Tax advisers and union-avoidance consulting firms would face new filing obligations or lose business.

drawbacks.text: The denial covers spending on lawful persuasion, including ordinary meetings and trainings where unions are discussed, so the effective cost of management's legal communications with its own employees rises — an asymmetry, since communications and expenditures by labor organizations are expressly excluded from the denial [S3].

Employers would face meaningful compliance burdens: distinguishing deductible from nondeductible spending, tracking wages and administrative costs tied to union-related meetings, and filing new information returns with penalties attached, plus Treasury would need to write new regulations within 240 days of enactment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The policy benefit to workers is real but indirect: raising the price of anti-union campaigns and forcing disclosure of the spending does not ban anything, it just stops the tax code from subsidizing it. The costs fall on employers and the administrative burden is significant, and the rule applies only one way — employer spending is penalized while union spending is not. Whether that asymmetry is fair depends on whether you view the starting point (employer campaigns against employee votes) as the problem the bill targets.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never scheduled a hearing or vote, and the bill died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Senator Casey introduced the bill on March 9, 2023 with 29 original cosponsors, all Democrats or allied independents [S1][S3][S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed [S5].
The 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025 without the bill advancing, so it did not become law [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that spend against union drives keep their tax deduction and their spending stays out of mandatory public reporting; union-avoidance consultants keep their roughly $340 million annual market. Workers get no change in the rules governing campaigns aimed at their union votes.

industries.note: The bill cites EPI figures that companies spend $340 million a year on outside consultants to sway workers' opinions about unions; making that spending nondeductible raises its price, and the bill would require such consultants to file information returns with the IRS.

industries.industry: Large employers that campaign against union drives
industries.note: They would lose a federal tax write-off for anti-union campaigns, captive-audience meetings, and related legal costs, and would have to report the spending with penalties for failures — raising the effective cost of opposing unionization.

Employer spending against organizing becomes more expensive and visible, improving the environment for union elections; the bill expressly excludes amounts paid by labor organizations from the deduction denial.
